title: AP CSP — Lesson 28 Homework: Bias & Crowdsourcing
notice: All questions are original. Q1–Q6 are AP-style practice, not official AP questions. Q7–Q12 and all marks are teacher-designed. Q5 earns one mark only for both correct choices and no others. Q5: select exactly TWO. All cases and numbers are synthetic. Show calculations and distinguish model results from real evidence.

questions.prompt: A fictional voluntary online survey gains many more responses from its existing users. What follows?

options.label: A
options.text: Representation is guaranteed.

options.label: B
options.text: More responses may preserve the same coverage gaps.

options.label: C
options.text: Non-users must be included.

options.label: D
options.text: Every response is accurate.

questions.explanation: B allows the same systematic omissions despite increased size. A assumes representation; C invents inclusion; D confuses quantity with accuracy.

questions.prompt: A fictional map ranks needs by raw report count. One person can resubmit the same report repeatedly. The main concern is:

options.label: A
options.text: The list must be sorted alphabetically.

options.label: B
options.text: All repeated observations are invalid.

options.label: C
options.text: The rule may reward repetition rather than need.

options.label: D
options.text: The Internet cannot carry many reports.

questions.explanation: C connects the chosen measure to a misleading ranking. A is unrelated; B overgeneralizes because distinct valid observations may repeat locations; D is not implied by the scenario.

options.label: A
options.text: Many residents submit observations through an online platform.

options.label: B
options.text: One computer repeats a calculation.

options.label: C
options.text: A programmer renames a local variable.

options.label: D
options.text: Two offline processors divide arithmetic tasks.

questions.explanation: A obtains input from many people via the Internet. B and C lack crowd input; D concerns computational work distribution rather than human contributions.

questions.prompt: Which fictional project best illustrates citizen science?

options.label: A
options.text: A store changes its logo.

options.label: B
options.text: A processor divides a file into packets.

options.label: C
options.text: Residents collect shade measurements for an online scientific study.

options.label: D
options.text: A developer tests only personal preferences.

questions.explanation: C involves distributed people contributing relevant research data, including non-scientists. A and D do not describe scientific participation; B is not human research contribution.

options.label: A
options.text: Deleting a region label always eliminates bias.

options.label: B
options.text: Comparing outcomes across groups can reveal a gap.

options.label: C
options.text: A large crowd guarantees true reports.

options.label: D
options.text: Improving coverage can reduce some bias without removing all bias.

questions.explanation: B describes an evaluation step; D states a bounded mitigation claim. A ignores related signals and data gaps; C ignores inaccurate contributions and selection effects.

questions.prompt: All listed access barriers are removed in a fictional model. Why might collected reports still be unrepresentative?

options.label: A
options.text: All enabled people must submit.

options.label: B
options.text: A valid file format proves representation.

options.label: C
options.text: People may differ in willingness or time to contribute.

options.label: D
options.text: Equal access forces identical opinions.

questions.explanation: C identifies a remaining participation mechanism. A equates opportunity with action; B concerns formatting rather than selection; D invents identical views.

questions.prompt: In a fictional map, only app users can report and ranking uses raw report counts. Identify one data bias risk and one design bias risk, then give a matched action for each.
questions.answer: Data risk: non-users are missing. Offer accessible alternative contribution routes with the same definitions. Design risk: repeated submissions inflate rankings. Detect duplicate submissions and evaluate whether the ranking better reflects valid evidence.
questions.explanation: Data risk: non-users are missing. Offer accessible alternative contribution routes with the same definitions. Design risk: repeated submissions inflate rankings. Detect duplicate submissions and evaluate whether the ranking better reflects valid evidence.

rubric.criterion: Identifies missing non-users as a data coverage risk.
Matches a relevant inclusion action to that coverage gap.
Identifies repeated submissions or activity being mistaken for need as a design risk.
Matches a rule or validation change to that design risk.

questions.prompt: Synthetic report rates: North 20%, South 80%. Sample A has 80 North and 20 South; B has 40 North and 60 South. Calculate each total report rate, give the difference in percentage points, and explain the cause.
questions.answer: A: (80×0.20 + 20×0.80)/100 = 32%. B: (40×0.20 + 60×0.80)/100 = 56%. B is 24 percentage points higher. Composition changes while the two group rates stay fixed.
questions.explanation: A: (80×0.20 + 20×0.80)/100 = 32%. B: (40×0.20 + 60×0.80)/100 = 56%. B is 24 percentage points higher. Composition changes while the two group rates stay fixed.

rubric.criterion: Correct sample A rate 32% with calculation.
Correct sample B rate 56% with calculation.
Correct difference of 24 percentage points.
Explains that the sample mix changes while group rates remain fixed.

questions.prompt: Synthetic population shares are North 60%, South 40%; report rates are 20%, 80%. Calculate the weighted rate, state the condition that keeps it fixed when the sample mix changes, and name one bias it does not remove.
questions.answer: 0.60×0.20 + 0.40×0.80 = 0.44 = 44%. It stays fixed while population shares and the two group rates remain fixed. It does not remove within-group nonresponse, self-selection or measurement bias.
questions.explanation: 0.60×0.20 + 0.40×0.80 = 0.44 = 44%. It stays fixed while population shares and the two group rates remain fixed. It does not remove within-group nonresponse, self-selection or measurement bias.

rubric.criterion: Uses the correct weighted sum with both population shares.
Obtains 44%.
States that both population shares and group rates remain fixed.
Names a relevant residual bias, such as within-group nonresponse or measurement error.

questions.prompt: Design a fictional online citizen-science shade study. State a research question, what distributed participants contribute using devices, one benefit of collaboration, and one matched quality check.
questions.answer: Question: how does shade coverage at sampled public stops change by time of day? Participants submit time-stamped observations using a common protocol on their devices. Many people can cover more locations or times. Audit a sample of observations against independent field checks.
questions.explanation: Question: how does shade coverage at sampled public stops change by time of day? Participants submit time-stamped observations using a common protocol on their devices. Many people can cover more locations or times. Audit a sample of observations against independent field checks.

rubric.criterion: States a suitable scientific research question.
Specifies relevant data contributed by distributed participants using computing devices.
Explains a plausible scale or collaboration benefit.
Gives a concrete quality check relevant to the contributed measurements.

questions.prompt: A fictional map accepts a report if its date and location fields are complete. Explain what this check can detect, what it cannot prove, one stronger verification step, and one remaining limitation.
questions.answer: It can detect missing required fields. It cannot prove the location was actually observed or the report is accurate. An independent field audit can check a sample. The audit may miss errors in unaudited reports.
questions.explanation: It can detect missing required fields. It cannot prove the location was actually observed or the report is accurate. An independent field audit can check a sample. The audit may miss errors in unaudited reports.

rubric.criterion: Identifies missing-field detection.
Distinguishes complete fields from accurate or genuine observations.
Proposes a relevant verification step using independent evidence.
States a specific remaining limitation of that step.

questions.prompt: Evaluate: “Crowdsourcing removes bias; our weighted 44% proves the real need.” The 44% comes from synthetic group shares and fixed report rates. Give two corrections, an inclusion action and a measure to evaluate that action.
questions.answer: Crowdsourcing can expand participation but does not guarantee representation or accurate input. The 44% summarizes assumptions, not verified real-world need. Offer supported contribution routes for missing participants. Compare who completes valid submissions before and after, while checking whether important groups remain absent.
questions.explanation: Crowdsourcing can expand participation but does not guarantee representation or accurate input. The 44% summarizes assumptions, not verified real-world need. Offer supported contribution routes for missing participants. Compare who completes valid submissions before and after, while checking whether important groups remain absent.

rubric.criterion: Corrects the claim that crowdsourcing removes bias.
Explains why synthetic weighted 44% does not prove real need.
Gives a specific action addressing an identified inclusion barrier.
Gives an observable measure that evaluates the action, rather than asserting guaranteed success.
